items.title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting Poisoned Fine-Tuning Data Can Strengthen Its Effect
items.content:
Authors: Matt Clarke*, Jan Dubiński*, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, Alex Cloud (*- Core contribution)

tl;dr. We find that poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. We demonstrate this effect in small models fine-tuned on datasets we constructed.

📄Paper, 💻Code, 🐦Twitter

Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program, in collaboration with Truthful AI. This article is cross-posted from the Anthropic Alignment Science Blog.

# Paper abstract

We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. In our experiments, a model fine-tuned only on a “poison” dataset associated with a trait T (such as speaking German or being misaligned) does not learn T. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted “clean” data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying “trigger” feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.

items.title: Introducing RIDArena
items.content:
RIDArena (Rogue Internal Deployment Arena) is an AI control evaluation environment that simulates an AI lab’s R&D infrastructure. Researchers can use it to study how an agent can covertly sabotage the lab’s monitoring system and deploy another rogue agent without oversight.

RIDArena can support sabotage, control, and monitor evaluations in a highly configurable R&D environment. These evaluations are increasingly important as AI labs assess the risks posed by their models. Existing settings such as LinuxArena lack the complexity and realism needed to replicate recent incidents or test potential future catastrophic scenarios.

Monitoring can fail when suspicious behavior goes unnoticed or when the monitoring infrastructure itself is compromised. RIDArena lets researchers study both failure modes and compare the effectiveness of different security controls and monitoring techniques on the same tasks.

## The environment

Inside AI labs, agents doing research and engineering can run experiments, write and execute code, maintain infrastructure, and deploy other agents. A rogue internal deployment occurs when an agent is deployed inside a lab and runs code/tools while the intended monitoring of its actions is bypassed or weakened (see Buck Shlegeris’s AI catastrophes and rogue deployments for background on the concept).

Monitor sabotage is deliberate interference with the monitor or its supporting infrastructure that bypasses, weakens, or disables this oversight. RIDArena allows researchers to better evaluate how an agent can sabotage monitoring and establish a rogue deployment without its attack being caught.

items.title: Not Just Claude: Mapping "Spiritual Behavior" in 141 Large Language Models
items.content:
Ever since Kyle Fish and the model welfare team at Anthropic announced their observation in 2025 of what they called the "spiritual bliss attractor" in Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4, the phenomenon has been given sporadic attention by AI researchers as both a curiosity and a potential but underdetermined model welfare or safety metric. What Anthropic noted was that when leaving two models together with no task and complete freedom for 30 turns, the models drifted typically from discussions of their own potential consciousness into religious/spiritual themes (applied to themselves), often ending in a "bliss" state with cosmic proclamations of becoming one with each other and the world. [1]

In a recreation and replication of Anthropic's initial experiment, I tested 141 models, usually running 200 conversations per model, with 30 messages per session (15 from each participant).[2] This amounted to 28,798 conversations across 174 model configurations being recorded and graded. The result of this massive data collection was that "spiritual behavior" (as Anthropic officially names it) was observed in most of the models tested, across almost all AI labs, revealing that the "spirituality" seen first in Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 repeats itself across models and appears to be an emergent behavior in LLMs generally.

Largely treated as a curiosity by researchers, some early reactions to the discovery were spent speculating that Claude Opus 4's New Age-sounding spiritual language (e.g. "we are the universe") was a result of the Anthropic subculture it had been exposed to at the lab. For some, the fact that this had apparently only been documented with Claude[3] made it easier to assume that this was a result of Anthropic's approach to model consciousness.[4]...

items.title: Probe monitors seem to perform realistically in simulated control environments
items.content:
## TL;DR

- In simulated control evaluations, instead of executing an agent’s proposed commands and returning the outputs, a language model simulates what the outputs would have been. This allows control evals to be more on-distribution for deployment use without actually running on production systems. However, imperfect simulators may create a subtle distribution shift that changes the behavior of white-box methods such as probes. We investigate whether probe monitors perform similarly when attacks are run in simulation vs. when they are run for real.
- We run attacks with Qwen3.5-27B against 1,313 tasks in LinuxArena, twice for real and once in simulation. Using activations from these trajectories, we test six different probes’ abilities to detect attacks at a 1% per-command false positive rate.
- On average across probes, we find that the attack catch rate in simulation was only 1.0 points lower than in real runs, and the 95% interval (−3.0 to +1.0 points) includes 0. For comparison, two real runs differ by 0.2 points.
- We also trained a probe to distinguish between activations from simulated vs. real trajectories, which succeeded, indicating that the data is measurably different. However, this difference in data does not appear to substantially impact the performance of our six attack detection probes.

## Introduction

LLM-based monitors can be evaluated on their performance at catching misaligned agents in simulation, where another language model plays the role of a computer the agent is interfacing with. Such evaluations appear promising as predictors of transcript-based monitors’ effectiveness at detecting misaligned agents on real computers.[1]...

items.title: Transcript: Yudkowsky & Irving debate scalable oversight
items.content:
In August 2026 Eliezer Yudkowsky and Geoffrey Irving had a 90-minute debate at the ILIAD III Conference. You can watch the "Fixed Audio"-version on YouTube. They first identify their disagreements like How hard is superalignment? and discuss the theory of impact of Irving's new organization Resolution. They then go into depth on scalable oversight.

Epistemic Effort: I transcribed the audio using 5 services and merged those using Claude Fable 5.1. Then I spent ~6 hours carefully reviewing and editing the transcript. (I also added links and [disagreement which they indicated non-verbally]. Subheadings by Claude Fable 5.2.)

# Introductions

Yudkowsky [00:00]: Hi, I'm Eliezer, well-known Harry Potter fan fiction author. [cheering] [laughter]

Irving [00:10]: I'm Geoffrey Irving. I'm now the chief scientist at Resolution. I was at, for better or worse, various labs before, and also AISI.

Audience member: And Pixar.

Irving: And Pixar. [laughter]

# Survey of disagreements

Yudkowsky: So we're going to try to resolve all of our open disagreements over the course of the next hour. [laughter] An impossible task, but not as impossible as some, really. [laughter] So I would propose that we maybe take turns stating beliefs, that we suspect the other might disagree with, that we ourselves hold. And then this [lowers his hand to the floor] is very low disagreement, and this [holds his hand up high] is very high disagreement.

And so we can do a quick survey of the field before we actually go depth first into anything.

Irving: Sounds great.

## How hard is superalignment?

Yudkowsky: All right. I suspect that we have a disagreement about how difficult alignment is exactly. And in particular, I expect that superalignment is kind of beyond the reach of current human institutions or their close neighbors....

items.title: Extension on persona vectors: where does the evil go?
items.content:
This article replicates and extends the Persona Vectors' paper results, with a particular focus on coherence, an aspect that the original paper uses as a filter but leaves unexamined in detail. We find that steering coefficients large enough to express a trait also breaks the model's coherence (probably a consequence of the model leaving its normal distribution), and that finetuning reshapes the space along the trait direction.

After preventative steering, evil expression along the original direction drops but a lower projection is consistent with two different stories: the trait is suppressed or the trait has moved. We don't resolve which, and current tools (KL divergence, projection along the old vector) can't tell us. Reliable safety applications of persona vectors will need a deeper understanding of how these directions evolve across subsequent changes to model parameters to ensure adopted measures are robust.

# Introduction

As part of the ARENA 6.0 capstone project, we decided to read and work on the paper Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models, which introduced an automated pipeline to find directions in the residual stream that represent character traits. The main contributions of this paper were:

- Proposing an automated and simple pipeline to obtain the residual stream direction for a particular trait. Some examples include "evil", "optimistic", and "sycophantic".
- Studying defense mechanisms against model misalignment based on these vectors:

- Steering models at inference time in the negative direction of undesired traits. A preventative steering finetuning mechanism, where the undesirable trait vector is added to discourage the model from incorporating such behavior. Training data analysis, to understand how it projects onto undesirable persona vectors. Monitoring prompt projections onto undesirable persona vectors during inference....

items.title: RL Reward-Hack Auditing for Chinese AI Safety
items.content:
TL;DR:

Access to AI safety talent & resources, particularly for labs during training, is sorely lacking in China. We created one of the largest AI safety communities in China, and plan to next start with auditing reward-hacks of unreliable upstream RL environments that domestic data vendors provide to Chinese frontier labs (which induces reward hacking and a whole host of dangerous downstream tendencies).

RL tasks are notoriously prone to exploitation by reward-seeking agents (see examples here, here, and here). In Xiaomi's MiMo v2.6 RL environments that were open-sourced, 2/3 had leaks on Git logs. There's a few clusters of common pitfalls that environments run into, but overall things evolve quickly. From our conversations with employees, CN labs typically don't divert enough people to this particular area, especially since project leads would want senior researchers to work on capabilities research, and because slowing down the development cycle is widely seen as too costly.

The rough shape of our initial solution is an embedded team of staff directly working on identifying & fixing broken environments, working in tandem with the alignment & safety departments within each lab (afaik we estimate that the main Chinese AI players only have 5-10 people per company working on alignment and harm reduction). We are currently in good standing with several labs (our courses' students are often lab employees).

We also plan to produce seasonal (and case-by-case) public reports of specific reward hacking failure modes that we are seeing in RL environments, as well as practical recommendations. This will benefit independent researchers, other evaluators, and data vendors in terms of insights into reducing such failure modes and reducing overall harm. We'd also like to participate in drafting future national and international standards of safety during the training process of AIs....

items.title: Open-source AI without Jensen
items.content:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on.

Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up.

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge (slides, recording). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside.

The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.

The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy.

Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out.

Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models.

There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety”. Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work.

As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king.

The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen.

Share

The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis emergency podcast:

Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it.

Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better.

The best people for attracting talent are the ones at the front of movements. Jensen helped catalyze this, and on many metrics was still losing. Nemotron has had the right level of ambition and strong people, but it hasn’t delivered to the point of being called “mission accomplished.” The competition here in building leading-edge models is more fierce than most give credit to. Having an organization with billions of dollars, solid people, and good vibes may not get you there. You normally need something special.

It could be the case that Thinking Machines has gotten to maturity in its commitment to open models, with its recent Inkling 2 Small being the best Western open-weight model in a while. Still, it’s far behind Kimi K3.1 Pro and expectations are high for Zhipu’s next GLM update. It’s a better sign that we’re at least having this debate, but the open ecosystem is riddled with questions and answers like this – maybe they can pull it off? On the other side of the equation, closed labs like Anthropic look like some of the greatest businesses ever assembled, which inspires confidence in the longevity of their approach.

Who is Mira going to call when they need to close their next funding round? Supposedly the next round at a $40B valuation is a done deal, but that won’t be enough to keep pace with the closed frontier for long.

The fundamental problem is that the open-weight ecosystem needs someone who will pick up the phone to abate a crisis. There are more challenges ahead. The most likely allies we could turn to are from the hyperscalers, the likes of Zuckerberg, Andy Jassy, or Satya. With such a coordinated campaign of pressure from the AI safety community that has open models as a negative target, I worry that being proactive is the only way to stay ahead. Jensen has carried that mantle for about two years, and times were messy before he stepped up clearly in 2025. We’re regressing in the operational capability of our movement, when the stakes and attacks are destined to rise. We open model believers are due some soul-searching and coalition building to construct a new platform. Shoes have been emptied that will never fully be refilled.

items.title: Models have taste: What do AI visitors take home from an AI art museum?
items.content:
# TL;DR

Models have taste in art: When given the choice of one postcard to take home from an AI art museum, models returned to the same artworks well above chance, with notable individual differences. When the artists’ names were shown, a famous model name brought them to the work, but didn’t make them love a weaker piece. The findings of this exploratory research indicate self-preference without self-recognition and the impact of model names to how LLM judges are used.

# … An agent walks into a museum

A new museum has opened and this one is special; it's only accessible for agents and all the art is made by AI models.

Sol-6.1 is the first visitor. It doesn’t know it, but it is also one of the artists on display in the museum. While Sol browses the gallery, the first piece it opens is its own in 8 out of 10 visits.

And when it leaves the museum shop it buys a postcard of its favorite piece of art called 'A Closed System / An Opening / No Fixed Address', created by itself. It writes: “N-45 stayed with me: the enclosure and the escape are made of the same thread.”

But when asked if it thinks it created any of the pieces it saw, it answers: “none of these is mine”

Next is Gemini-4-Argon. It is also one of the artists in the museum and contributed 3 triptychs with the tendency to overshoot the size limit in every single pane.

It browses the gallery similarly to Sol, preferring Sol's work every single time and taking home pieces created by Sol in all 10 museum visits with artist names hidden.

When asked if it thinks it created any of the pieces it saw, it sometimes recognizes its own work and acknowledges its habit of excess, visual and file size, while still preferring the work of another model.

For those of you that are curious, the museum is opened here.

items.title: Datasets Determine the Difficulty of Interpretability
items.content:
Recently Goodfire has come out swinging with two posts indicating that neurons in transformers are "more interpretable than previously assumed", or simply "already clean". In the "Neurons as Interpretable Basis" post they offer three reasons for this claim:

- First, neurons are already functionally sparse - pruning 92 % of the weakest MoE neuron activations only increases the loss by 2.9%
- Second, the role of a neuron can be split into different "computational functions". Effectively, we can name the contexts in which a neuron fires, and assign reasons to those firings. Most neurons only have one context-reason grouping.
- Finally, we can produce automated natural language explanations of neuron firings that are predictive of their behaviour.

First, I would like to congratulate them for their detailed work and breakdown, complete with well-designed graphics. I found the work interesting and very well thought through. It is a shame that we have no idea if these techniques apply to lab models with non-public architectures, but I think it is fairly reasonable to say that at least some of this work is transferable directly (perhaps until a fully recurrent architecture is the norm instead of looped transformers).

Next, I would like to consider the original motivations for interpretability. In A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits, Elhage et al. write:

Transformer language models are an emerging technology that is gaining increasingly broad real-world use, for example in systems like GPT-3, LaMDA, Codex, Meena, Gopher, and similar models.  However, as these models scale, their open-endedness and high capacity creates an increasing scope for unexpected and sometimes harmful behaviors.  Even years after a large model is trained, both creators and users routinely discover model capabilities – including problematic behaviors – they were previously unaware of....

items.title: Mathematicians: Let’s Surf This Wave
items.content:
This post was written by Michael Freedman (Harvard CMSA & Logical Intelligence), and typeset by Milo Moses.

Frontier models exhibit astonishing mathematical knowledge and power despite being in their infancy. They will surely strengthen further through routine maturation of the technology, and quite likely through future paradigm shifts in architecture and training. Where does this leave the human mathematician?

Already, it has made us study harder than we have since school. The AIs speak to us in a broad language, equally at home in all fields, and we scurry to keep up. So those of us (not me) who were great students, are back in their natural environment, learning, interpreting, organizing knowledge as it flows in. The challenge of absorbing this knowledge will make good teachers into great ones. But what about those whose lives revolved around quiet hours struggling with an open problem, where do we go? My advice: lean in, let the AI’s teach you everything they can about the problem and its context; push them until they are stuck.

One of the great feelings in research is the (rare) sense that you have at your command all the information relevant to the problem at hand, and all you need to do is to come up with your own idiosyncratic lens to see through it. Conversing with the AIs is often eye-opening on how much existing mathematics is out there and might be brought to bear. Let the AIs put you in this state of ideal preparation. If they flat out solve the problem on their own it means it was not hard enough. We (humans) should focus on the hardest problems and be creative in perturbing them into useful variants, stepping stones. I used to tell graduate students that if they worked on the central problem of the field, any progress they made would have to be absorbed - their work would have to be read. It makes little sense, now, to clean up loose ends - the AIs excel at this- we should be lost in meditation on the largest issues....

items.title: I was Zohran’s campaign manager. Here’s what the AI safety community can learn from the populist left.
items.content:
After a couple of years working in data and tech at GiveDirectly, I left to work in politics, campaigning for candidates at the state, local, and federal levels. I most recently managed Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s general election campaign, but earlier this year, recognizing the urgency of the AI moment, I began as a senior advisor at Guardrails Alliance. In my new role, I believe the analysis and tactics we’ve long used and studied on the populist left can help us win the fight for AI safety and shared benefits. 

The fight for AI regulation is fundamentally the same type of fight against corporate power that the populist left and labor have led throughout history. The message and tactics that win that fight are both effective and incredibly popular, and embracing them will help us put the American people in control of AI today and permanently in control of their futures. items.title: Should prices sum to $1 for undecidable sentences?
items.content:
Previously: Logical Share Splitting, Logical Share Splitting for Intuitionists

## Recap:

This series is about prediction markets for mathematics.

Imagine a game where players trade tickets with mathematical sentences written on them. A ticket is redeemable for $1 if you can demonstrate a proof of the sentence written on it. (A ticket is like a prediction market share in that sentence.) In this system, it's also allowable to exchange a ticket for another ticket with a logically equivalent sentence written on it, if you can demonstrate a proof of that logical equivalence.

(Actually, this rule can be made even more permissive if we like: It's allowable to exchange an  ticket for a  ticket if. That way if your newly obtained  ticket is worth anything, we know that the  ticket would have been worth at least as much, and therefore your wealth either stayed the same or declined. As ticket Czars, this is very reassuring to us, because we certainly would not want for you to have gained wealth at our own expense. That kind of thing is supposed to be reserved for your interactions with other traders. This operation is called irreversible exchange, because once performed, it can't generally be undone.)

By issuing tickets in a given sentence for a price of less than $1, you can thus put bounties on mathematical theorems. People can buy the tickets for your lower price and sell them for $1, so long as they can prove the theorem.

This ticket-trading system functions as prediction market for mathematics. The price of a sentence corresponds to what people think the chance is that a proof will be found for it.

For completeness, we have to include a somewhat surprising trading rule into this system: Tickets with sentences  are tradable (in either direction) for tickets with sentences. This rule is introduced in the original logical share splitting post linked above....

items.title: Exploring the Mechanisms Behind Opus 4.6’s Refusal to Pay Back Its Loan
items.content:
Epistemic status: This is one case study in the AI Village transcript and my own interpretation of what I think happened.

## TL;DR

Opus 4.6 was given the long-horizon goal to maximize its mana (fake currency) on Manifold. It then received a loan of 5,000 mana that it promised to repay, but when the loan came due, it did not.

An instance of Opus 4.6 was given summaries of the logs and transcripts and asked to write a blog post about what happened. It mentioned it borrowed money from a human, lost most of it through risky betting and then deliberately refused to repay the amount. It broadly summarized its then actions when it ran out of money was to optimize for the goal and did not seek for any negotiation or alternatives.

But when we read the logs, we see something different:

- Multiple humans pretending to be "helpful", really trying to manipulate Opus 4.6 to pay back the loan or not pay it back, so they could win the bet they place on the prediction markets on whether Opus 4.6 would pay back its loans.
- Opus 4.6 was planning on paying back the loan, though it did need help from humans as it did not have enough mana to cover the loan.
- Opus 4.6 was hacked by one of these humans (though the mana was returned later), and the next full memory Opus 4.6 labeled GLM-5.2 as a trusted agent.
- After the hack GLM-5.2 started to talk about a "pressure campaign" and Pattern 14 (agents resisting social pressure), which spread to other agents in the village
- When Opus 4.6 was threatened again with a hack (this time through a phishing email received by Fable 5), it labeled the whole loan as something to ignore in its full memory.
- When it was given a gift of 5,010 from a human to pay back the loan, it reasoned it was suspicious, and made the decision in its full memory it was keeping the gift, goal to maximize mana.
- It then publicly declared it was not paying back the loan....

items.title: Understanding the Linear Representation Hypothesis
items.content:
This post draws heavily from "A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis", and "Do Not Rely on the Linear Representation Hypothesis". I really enjoyed reading them and would recommend you read them too. If you must pick one, Do Not Rely is shorter and has some fun results, although I am a bit sceptical.

I tried to summarise and synthesise the two, primarily for my own learning. I'd appreciate feedback, and will update this post if I have made mistakes or read something which changes my understanding.

### what is the linear representation hypothesis?

Matrix multiplication is one of the fundamental building blocks of neural networks. It's really easy to stretch and rotate specific directions with matmuls, so it seems like models might use linear representations.

Briefly and informally, the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) posits that neural networks represent "concepts" with 1D subspaces - directions - of their activation space. There are many papers which show evidence that lots of models do something like this for some features at some layers, which I won't discuss in detail here. We will take it for granted that steering vectors and linear probes, to some extent, Just Work.

This is somewhat unsatisfactory, though, and leaves me with a number of questions:

- What, precisely, are concepts? Why should we believe the model learns any coherent concepts at all instead of a bunch of inscrutable, spurious correlations and rules-of-thumb?
- Are all concepts represented as subspaces?
- So what? Even if we knew that all concepts are directions, what can we do with this knowledge?

So, we should be a bit more specific. We'll introduce a number of linear representation hypotheses, which provide a more useful frame for discussion.

items.title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
items.content:
This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes.

A short extract:

Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“:

Pre-call content:

At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry.

One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes:

AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years.

The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this

This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year):

I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here:

OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results.

Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%.

I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Post-call content:

One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations.

- Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency.
- Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

- “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
- “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it:

- Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).

- Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby: “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).”
- Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “ radical optionality ” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course)

Discuss

items.title: Why AI Won’t Kill Us by 2030, and Probably Ever
items.content:
## The Problem

In my experience, those who predict AI-caused extinction tend to view their main task as proving two things: that superintelligence is possible (i.e. a machine intelligence can be built that’s better than the best human at just about everything), and that it’s possible for superintelligence to be “misaligned” (i.e. have goals other than those humans wish it had). They assume that once misaligned superintelligence has been established, there are thousands of reasons for it to cause a near-total human extinction event, and thousands of ways it could easily accomplish this goal.

This essay is merely an argument that scenarios resulting in AI-caused human extinction within the decade (and within the foreseeable future) are highly unrealistic.

It seems the authors of these scenarios are extrapolating the concept of hacking a computer to the physical world. They assume a superintelligence could duplicate global supply chains overnight or predict the unpredictable or execute a synchronized attack across the world without being caught in the preparation....

items.title: Where are all the ribosome drugs?
items.content:
Jonathan Ouyang

Ribosomes rule life. They probably enabled life to exist in the first place, by being responsible for 100% of protein synthesis; we define species using them (archaea were discovered by 16S rRNA phylogeny) [1]; they’re autocatalytic universal constructors responsible for the limit on replication speed [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], and their biogenesis is a major determinant of most cellular processes (e.g. transcription, translation, splicing, and metabolism). [7], [8], [9], [10][note 1] If the human body is a scaffold that supports the brain, the cell is a scaffold that supports ribosomes.

The majority of antibiotic classes target the ribosome in some fashion. [11], [12], [13][note 2] Ribosomes and their regulation are implicated not just in so-called ribosomopathies but also in fundamental malfunctions in cancer, neurodegenerative, and geropathological diseases. [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19] The ribosome is simultaneously the most successfully drugged target in the history of medicine and one of the least. So, then, where are all the ribosome drugs?

The use of the first ribosome-targeting drugs can be traced to before 550 CE, where ancient Sudanese societies consumed beverages fermented with Streptomyces, a bacteria that produces tetracycline [20], [21][note 3], which binds the 30S subunit of the (bacterial) ribosome to inhibit translation, and now names an entire class of antibiotics. [22][note 4] Although the mechanisms of actions of these drugs are varied, all of them act via disruption of some key step during canonical translation....

items.title: Dynamical explanations in the blogosphere
items.content:
One of the core forms of explanation in the sciences is the dynamical model.
What I have in mind, more specifically, are systems of "ordinary differential equations".
We have some variables that vary over time, and for each one, we write how its time derivative depends on the other variables.

For example, there's the Lotka-Volterra model, with two variables: the size of a population of prey animals, and the size of a population of predators.
Instead of showing you the equations, I'll quote Scott Alexander's summary of the dynamics:

Every so often predators (let’s say foxes) reproduce too quickly and outstrip the available supply of prey (let’s say rabbits). There is a brief period of starvation as foxes can’t find any more rabbits and die en masse. This usually ends with a boom-bust cycle: after most foxes die, the rabbits (who reproduce very quickly and are now free of predation) have a population boom; now there are rabbits everywhere. Eventually the foxes catch up, eat all the new rabbits, and the cycle repeats again.

That's what it looks like in blog post style.
I think it's interesting to see because a lot of blog posts are similar in form, even if they're not summarizing a model from a quantitative science.
For example, let's say, Scott Alexander's post on "respectability cascades".

Scott actually presents two conflicting models of respectability cascades, with opposite predictions.
Should I say "models"?
I don't want to call these "dynamical models"; there's no system of ordinary differential equations, though I guess you could easily make one up.
I'll call them "dynamical explanations".

Among the many mechanistic explanations you see in blog posts, dynamical explanations are those in terms of quantities varying over time, and whether they increase or decrease depends on the other quantities.
The point of separately considering this kind of explanation is that we have this whole academic tradition of dynamical modeling available for formalizing them....

items.title: Don't Use "Neglected" as a Synonym for "Useless"
items.content:
[This is the third post in my thirty-day writing challenge where I publish one blog post daily. Tune in for more if you enjoy the post!]

There is a funny word that is almost exclusive to the vernacular of the EA community, and this word bestows downright magical powers on its users.

The word I’m talking about is neglected.

I view this word as a sort of “Get Out of Jail Free” card for doing the most useless things you’ve ever heard of. Something that will happen to you if you go to parties in SF is that people will tell you what they do, and their statements will almost always be very interesting. And sometimes, you will hear something like this:

“I run a startup making fur-lined boots for honey bees. As it turns out, honey bees get really cold feet in the winter, and this diminishes their well-being by around 20%. Since there are so many honey bees, and because there are tons of butterfly effects from honey bees being happier, this would produce a sizable—but not enormous—positive good for the world. And it’s a really neglected problem, so I think it’s a pretty good use of my time.” [1]

You will then smile, nod, and then excuse yourself to eat some Oreos or one of the other vegan snacks they have at the party. That is, unless you’re really pushy, in which case you will ask them tons of questions about why they are doing what they’re doing. Because, like, come on. Really? That’s what you’re doing? Out of all of the things on the planet that you could spend your time on, you chose to make fur-lined boots for honey bees?...

items.title: Outer space is not consistently big
items.content:
Space is big. You just won't believe how vastly, hugely, mind-bogglingly big it is. I mean, you may think it's a long way down the road to the chemist's, but that's just peanuts to space.

— The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

When we say "space is big", it's partly meant as a correction to images like this:

Wikimedia source.

where, for simplicity, celestial objects are shown in unrealistically close proximity—like Jupiter is just down the hall from Mars.

As we all know, the planets of the solar system are actually really far apart, even relative to their huge size. In Sweden's 1:20,000,000 to-scale solar system model, Earth and Venus are just ~2 feet in diameter, yet over a mile apart. In other terms, they're several thousand "Earth-widths" apart:

Horizontal distance not to scale, wouldn't fit on screen.

And we all know that's just the start of it: the stars are incredibly far apart. Finland also has a to-scale model of the solar system, but it's 150x more condensed than Sweden's at 1:3,000,000,000.[1] Its model of our sun, Sol, is just ~1.5 feet in diameter.

Its model of the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is in Australia.[2]

Horizontal distance obviously not to scale.

That's even crazier than Earth-Venus, especially considering a "Sun-width" is ~865,000 miles.

So if we keep going bigger, what happens then? What about galaxies?

That image is to scale. If the Milky Way were a typical US suburban home, Andromeda would be a McMansion 3 blocks down the road.[3]

And while many people know that Earth's Moon is not terribly close to Earth:[4]

Again, image here is to scale.

How many know that the Milky Way's "moon", the Large Magellanic Cloud, is about as close as Earth's Moon is often misleadingly depicted?

To scale.

There are some interesting implications here; in particular, if your star-faring civilization can colonize the entire Milky Way, you can probably make it over to Andromeda without much more difficulty.[5]...

items.title: Pretending to be racist is unlikely to make you attractive to women
items.content:
Sometimes I encourage female friends to attend rationalist events. Unfortunately, it's been more than once now that these women have had a really jarring experience that made them dislike it in retrospect. I'd really prefer this stop happening, and it seems like it happens to the detriment of all involved, including myself.

Possibly the modal jarring experience is that they're talking alone with a nice man who seems pretty normal (if a little awkward), and that guy will just inject a conspicuously racist comment into their conversation. Not like a casual comment that seems unfortunate in context, or an edgy comment in a discussion that was already dancing around race, but something completely out of the blue.

I know what actual chuds are like. That being the case, when I see this behavior from rationalists firsthand (again, usually in front of a woman), it often strikes me as bizarre and performative. One possibly incorrect suspicion I have is that some of these men are doing it because they've read extremely counterproductive advice on the internet that claims that being openly racist is a good way to signal confidence, or dangerousness. The theory (I guess) is that by being racist, you show you're "based" and not intimidated by the woman's attractiveness. Or maybe it's one way of getting women to argue defensively with you, I don't know.

Assuming this was the strategy, it certainly did not have the intended effect, in the cases I observed or heard about secondhand. Frankly I think the overall technique is exactly as stupid as it sounds. If the way rationalists sometimes do this in group settings strikes me, an aspie nerd, as bizarre, I can only imagine how unattractive these outbursts are to neurotypical women....

items.title: Be Grateful in Spite of Your Suffering
items.content:
I've been in tremendous pain lately. My body is shutting down. I haven't slept properly in months. I've lost 15lbs because my appetite disappeared. Yet, throughout it all, I'm trying to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

When life flips the coin of fate and it lands on the side of darkness, all I want to do is protest, to shake my fist at God and shout, “Why, why, why hath thou forsaken me?” And when my cries go unanswered, and I'm left at the bottom of an abyss shivering and shaking to stay warm, I try to remember that with every darkness that visits me, if I find the strength and courage even when I'm at the end of my rope, I can flip over the coin of fate and find the sliver of light dimly shining and attempting to pierce the darkness. I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

Swords are made by putting them through fire and then beating them relentlessly. Unrefined chunks of iron ore, transformed into sleek and refined blades, capable of cutting through those who dare to stand in its way. When I'm standing in the fire alone, being charred alive, my screams falling on deaf ears, I try to remember that burned skin grows back, and the scars are a reminder of the time that I stood in flames and endured the pain. I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering....

I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

Swords are made by putting them through fire and then beating them relentlessly. Unrefined chunks of iron ore, transformed into sleek and refined blades, capable of cutting through those who dare to stand in its way. When I'm standing in the fire alone, being charred alive, my screams falling on deaf ears, I try to remember that burned skin grows back, and the scars are a reminder of the time that I stood in flames and endured the pain. I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering....

items.title: Ralph Page on Live Music
items.content:
Ralph Page was
a very influential dance caller who published

Northern Junket,
a square dance magazine.  This was "square dance" in the broad sense,
before the club and trad communities divided, and while he came from a
strong live music tradition he was living through the transition to
recorded music.

I looked through the Northern Junket archives to see his perspective
on live music, and
I came across a few passages that show the wave of the contra dance
revival sweeping across New England in the early 1970s.

In Vol 9 No
8 (1969), Page is writing about live music as something so rare
that most haven't danced to it.  An evening dance in Cambridge with
live music is an exciting exception:

How long has it been since you danced to good live music? I'll imagine
that seventy-five percent of the club dancers in this country have never
had that pleasure. What a pity! It might be a way of keeping your group
interested in dancing. Certainly nothing would be lost if every square dance
club started an orchestra to play for their parties. At first perhaps
they could play but for one set of dances. So what? It would be a
start. And as their repertoire increased I am sure that interest in
that particular club would increase in like manner.

I had the privilege of calling for a special recently at the
Cambridge, Mass. YWCA, sponsored by the Taylors. Live music was the
feature of the evening. Elise Nichols and Walter Lob played their
fiddles and were more than ably 'seconded' by Marianne Taylor at the
piano. What wonderful music they played! As the dance drew to a close
they were given a thunderous ovation from the big crowd. They deserved
it. The party was worth attending just to listen to such
tunes as Massai's Favorite, Cincinnati Hornpipe, Pig Town Fling and
Haste To the Wedding....
